activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: To clear a fraction from an equation, multiply both sides by its denominator: if x divided by 3 equals 5, multiplying both sides by 3 gives x = 15.
story:
The library was quiet except for the pencil sharpener grinding somewhere near the biography section. Noemie spread her worksheet on the table and stared at the problem Ms. Francis had circled in red: x divided by 3 equals 5. She had solved every other one, the ones like x plus 4 equals 9, just by undoing the plus. This one had a fraction sitting in the way, and she did not know how to move it.

Tatiana dropped into the chair across from her and slid over a wrinkled receipt. "Augustin's at the vending machine," she said. "We owe him. He paid for all three of us at the cafe after the science fair, and now we have to pay him back, but the receipt got wet and the total smeared." The bottom of the paper was a molten gray blot where the ink had run. Tatiana tapped the surviving line above it. "My share was 5 dollars. We split it three ways, so we each paid the same."

"So the total is some number," Noemie said slowly, "and if you divide it by 3, you get 5." She pulled the receipt toward her and wrote on the back, where the paper was still clean. "That is the same as my worksheet. X divided by 3 equals 5." She looked at the smeared blot, then at her pencil. The total was hidden, but if she could work backward from the share, she could find it.

She tried things out loud. "If the total were 12, each share would be 4, because 12 divided by 3 is 4. That does not coincide with 5 dollars, so 12 is wrong." She tested 18 in her head; 18 divided by 3 was 6, still wrong. Then she wrote a 3 next to both sides of her equation, one on the left and one on the right, like weights matched on a scale. The fraction on the left cleared away, and on the right, 3 times 5 stood alone. "Fifteen," she said. "The total is 15 dollars." She checked it the opposite direction: 15 divided by 3 was exactly 5.

Augustin came back from the vending machine cracking open a bag of pretzels. Tatiana held out the receipt. "Fifteen dollars," she said. "Five each, three of us." Augustin counted on his fingers, shrugged, and dug into his pocket.

Noemie turned back to her worksheet. She copied the same move onto the circled problem, wrote a 3 on both sides, and watched the fraction disappear. Ms. Francis passed the table on her way to the reference shelf, glanced down, and put a small check mark next to it with her red pen. Noemie flipped to the next problem, which had a 4 in the denominator instead, and picked up her pencil again. "Four goes on both sides," she said to Tatiana. "Watch."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
story:
Charles had taped his hypothesis to the top of the display board in big letters: seeds watered with leftover tea will sprout faster than seeds watered with plain water. The science fair was two days away, and the evidence said otherwise. Every plain-water cup on the windowsill of the science classroom had a green hook of a sprout poking through the soil. Every tea-water cup held nothing but damp dirt.

"No, no, no," Charles said. He leaned over the tray until his breath foged the plastic wrap. He had done everything right. Same soil, same number of seeds, same squirts from the same dropper. He lifted a tea cup and sniffed it, getting a bitter wet-teabag smell, and set it down harder than he meant to.

Ludovik looked up from his own project across the lab table, where he was gluing cotton balls to a poster about static electricity. "Maybe they just need more time."

"They got the same time as the others. That's the whole point." Charles rubbed the back of his neck. Something he couldn't see had to be going on in those cups, or something he hadn't thought of. Maybe the seeds were duds. He dug one out of the dirt with a pencil tip and found it swollen and split, exactly like the sprouting ones. So the seeds were alive. The tea itself had to be the difference, though he couldn't watch that part happening. He planted six fresh seeds, three in each group, watered them, and labeled them "Trial Two" with a shaking marker.

Alexi came in from gym class still carrying the smell of the locker room and peered at the trays. "Why does half your window look like a graveyard?"

"Because my hypothesis is wrong, probably." Charles said it quietly, like testing whether the words were true.

By the next morning, Trial Two had copied Trial One exactly. The plain-water seeds had cracked open and pushed up pale white stems; the tea seeds had swelled and stopped. Charles sat down on the radiator and put his head in his hands. His Saturday, his careful notes, all of it had gone toward proving himself wrong, and it felt like he had nothing to show.

Ms. Oyelaran stopped at his table on her way to unlock the supply cabinet. She looked at the board, then at the trays, then at him. "Present it," she said.

"Present a fail?"

"A wrong result is still a real result," she said, and moved on to argue with Ludovik about the cotton balls.

Charles stared at his notebook. He had recorded every watering, every measurement. Nobody else would know this, that too much tea stops sprouts cold, or whatever it was doing down there in the dark. It was a small thing to know, but it was real, and he had proved it twice. Being vain about his first guess would be the actual failure.

He picked up the marker, crossed out nothing, and printed a new line under the old hypothesis: "Prediction not supported. Findings reported." Then he stepped back to look at the board, the ghost of the tea smell still on his fingers.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: In the beep test, or multistage fitness test, runners go back and forth between markers usually 20 meters apart, and the beeps come faster at each new level.
story:
The whistle blew, and the cones at each end of the gym looked very far apart, like they were trying to depict the distance across an actual desert. Beatrice stood on the starting line with eleven other girls, all of them trying out for the track team, and waited for the first beep.

"Twenty meters," Mikaela whispered beside her. "You run to the far line before the next beep, then back. It's the multistage fitness test, but everybody just calls it the beep test."

"What happens after a while?" Beatrice asked.

"New levels. And the beeps come faster at each one."

The first beep sounded, and everyone shuffled forward at an easy jog. It was almost funny, how slow it felt. Beatrice had finished her sprint warm-ups early just to be first in line, and now she had nothing to do with all that energy. Last spring, at soccer tryouts, she had sprinted the opening drill like a maniac, gasped her way through the middle, and been cut before the final round. The coach had said something about pacing, and she had hated hearing it.

The beeps guided them back and forth, back and forth. At level two, Beatrice noticed she was arriving at each line several steps early, standing there waiting. So was a tall girl named Ryerson, bouncing on her toes. Ahead of them, a few girls ran hard every single leg, arriving exactly on the beep, breathing like they'd already run a race.

Beatrice thought about the pattern she could feel but not see: the beeps were a clock, and the clock was speeding up. If the beeps came faster at each new level, then the girls sprinting now were spending something they would need later. But waiting too long was dangerous too, because once the beeps outran a comfortable jog, she would have to sprint just to survive, with no cushion left.

She tested it. For the rest of level two, she aimed to arrive two steps before each beep, no more. It took constant adjusting, like pouring water into a glass without spilling. Ryerson, beside her, kept bursting and stopping, bursting and stopping.

Level four arrived with an ominous silence, then a quicker rhythm. The sprinters ahead began to look ragged. One girl missed a beep twice and was waved to the side. Ryerson reached level five but shook her head, hands on knees, and stepped off.

By level six it was just Beatrice and two others, and there was no pacing left, only running. Her lungs burned. The far line swam toward her, then away, then toward her again.

The final beep she caught by a lunge, one hand slapping the floor.

"Good," said Ms. MacLeod, checking her clipboard. "Wednesday, four o'clock, first practice."

Beatrice walked to the water fountain on legs that felt like static, and Mikaela was already there, holding a cup out to her.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: People with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms.
story:
Alicia sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with a tissue pressed to her nose, trying to breathe through the congestion and failing. Her mother had finally dragged her in after four days of fever, and now she had time to think. Her thoughts kept circling back to the sleepover at Shania's house, six days ago. Everyone had been perfectly healthy that night. They had eaten pizza, watched a movie, and shared one big bowl of popcorn, passing it around the circle.

"Pizza and popcorn, that's it," said a voice, and Alicia looked up. Sebastian was sitting two chairs down, red-nosed and miserable, wrapped in his own coat.

"What are you doing here?" she asked.

"Same thing you are, probably. My mom says it's the flu." He sneezed into his elbow. "Weird, because Shania's sleepover was the only place I went all week, and nobody there was sick."

Alicia frowned. That was the strange part. Shania had hosted them all, and she had seemed fine, full of energy, doing handstands in the hallway. But Sebastian had the flu, Alicia had the flu, and by now she knew from the group chat that two other girls from the sleepover had it too. Four out of five guests, and the one who wasn't sick was Sebastian's little sister, who had fallen asleep early and hadn't shared the popcorn.

"Wait," Alicia said slowly. "Four of us got sick and we all arrived the same day. If we caught it there, somebody had to have it at the sleepover."

"Nobody was coughing," Sebastian said.

"But what if you can spread the flu before you even know you have it?" Alicia pulled out her phone and typed carefully, and there it was: people with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms. She held the screen so Sebastian could see. "So Shania could have been coming down with it that night and looked totally healthy."

Sebastian groaned. "Then Shania got us sick without knowing. She's going to feel awful."

"She didn't do anything wrong," Alicia said. She tried to console him. "It wasn't like she was careless. She didn't even know."

The nurse called Sebastian's name first, and he stood up, shrugging his coat back onto his shoulders. "When we're better, we should tell everyone at school. People always blame whoever sneezes, but it might be the person who looks fine."

Alicia nodded and pulled up the group chat. She started typing a message to Shania, asking how she was doing, and added a thumbs-up emoji at the end before pressing send.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: The turnaround is the end of the twelve-bar form, usually landing on the V chord, which pulls the music back to the start of the next chorus.
story:
The music room smelled like valve oil and old carpet, and Mr. Bautista had written twelve empty boxes on the whiteboard. "Count them as we play," he said. "Blues form is twelve bars, then it starts over." Annabelle had her trumpet on her lap. She had never made up a solo before, and every note she knew suddenly felt like it belonged to someone else.

Ira sat at the piano, which was the problem, because Ira wanted the solo for himself. He had asked twice already, and Mr. Bautista had said the same thing twice: "Annabelle's turn today. You comp the chords." Ira plunked the first four bars with his whole forearm, sulky, then settled down and used actual chords. Behind them, Eliot tapped the rhythm on his knees and told a long anecdote about his cousin who once got lost during a concert and played the wrong song for a whole minute. "That will not happen to me," Annabelle said, and then it did.

She lost count somewhere in bar six. She kept playing, but her notes stopped matching what Ira's hands were doing, and the sound went wrong in a way she could hear but not see. She stopped, mouthpiece at her lip, and listened. The chords moved through a pattern, round and round, and near the end the sound seemed to lean, as if the whole progression were tipping forward. "There," she said. "What's that bit?"

"The turnaround," Eliot said.

She watched Ira's hands through the next chorus and tracked it. The turnaround was the end of the twelve-bar form, and it landed on the V chord, which pulled the music back to the start of the next chorus. She had a theory: if she got lost again, she didn't need to count, she only needed to wait for that tipping sound and jump in when the form started over. She could test it right now, before the fear of getting lost went extinct in her mind the way courage sometimes did, five minutes after you needed it.

"Take it from the top," she said. "And Ira, play the turnaround loud so I can hear it coming." Ira had changed his mind about the solo, or at least about her having it. He played the twelve bars clean and strong, and at bar twelve he leaned into the V chord like a door swinging open. Annabelle came through it on an F, loud, right on the downbeat of the next chorus, and held it until the room went bright around her. "Again," she said.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place.
story:
Evelyn spread the photocopy across the library table so flat that the corners stopped curling. It was a page from a settler's diary, written in 1846 by a woman named Margaret Hale, and Evelyn's assignment was to explain why the Hale family left Missouri for Oregon. The trouble was that the diary didn't come out and say why. Nobody in 1846 wrote essays for thirteenth-grade students to digest.

"Read this part again," Leilani said, dragging her chair closer. She tapped a paragraph with one finger. "'The bank took our claim in the spring, and Josiah cannot find work in Hannibal. Yet the papers say Oregon soil is black as coffee and a man may hold six hundred acres.'"

Madelynn arrived late, holding a note from the coach and still in her practice jersey, because she wanted to keep her eligibility and that meant showing Ms. Rao she was actually studying. She dropped into the third chair and squinted at the page. "That's two different kinds of reasons," she said. "Bad stuff at home, good stuff out there."

Evelyn wrote two columns in her notebook. At the top of one she wrote AWAY, and at the top of the other she wrote TOWARD. "The bank taking the claim goes under away," she said. "It pushed them out. The free land goes under toward. It pulled them." She worked down the diary, sorting line by line. The fever that took the baby went under away. The letters from a cousin in Oregon went under toward. Then she hit a sentence about wolves and hesitated, because wolves in Missouri could push you, but so could wolves in Oregon pull you back. "Madelynn, which column?"

Ms. Rao passed behind them on her way to the returns cart and paused just long enough to see the page. "There's a name for those," she said. "Push factors and pull factors." Then she went on shelving, which was her way of saying figure out the rest yourselves, and Evelyn underlined the two words at the top of her columns.

By the last paragraph Evelyn noticed something that made her sit back. The pull factors were the ones Margaret Hale wrote about longest, the black soil, the six hundred acres, but the push factors were what got them moving. Her own family had moved two years ago, and Evelyn had always told people it was because of the new job, which was a pull factor if anything was. But her mother had also been laid off, and somehow they never mentioned that part. It felt arbitrary, which reason you named when people asked. Maybe there wasn't one true reason. Maybe there was a whole column.

"There's a third problem," Leilani said, pointing at the diary's last line. "'We turned back at the river and will try again in spring.'" Evelyn looked at it for a long moment, then wrote one more heading under her columns: TOO SCARED TO MOVE YET. Madelynn laughed so loudly that Ms. Rao looked over, and Evelyn slid the notebook out of view and started copying the columns onto her poster paper.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Frying whole spices briefly in hot oil or ghee, called tempering or tadka in Indian cooking, releases their flavour into the fat.
story:
The recipe card on Anna's station had three jobs on it: rice, curry, flatbread. All three had to reach the table at the same time, which meant the rice had to start first because it took twenty minutes, the curry in the middle, and the flatbread last, cooked fast in the dry pan. She wrote the order on the back of her hand with a pen she'd negotiated off Freyja in exchange for the last of the paprika.

"That's not a plan, that's a tattoo," Freyja said.

"It's an algorithm," Anna said. "Step one, step two, step three, and dinner comes out all at once."

Ms. Henry moved between the stations, saying nothing unless someone's pan was actually on fire, which so far it wasn't. Anna got the rice bubbling, then turned to the curry and read the first line again. Heat the ghee, add the cumin seeds, fry them briefly until they darken, then add the onions. She frowned at it. Why fry the seeds first, alone in the fat, instead of stirring them in later with everything else? They were going to get cooked anyway. She thought of last term, when she'd dumped cinnamon straight into her porridge and tasted nothing but pale powder. Maybe the seeds had to go into hot fat on their own for some reason she couldn't see.

"I'm going to test it," she told Theodore at the next station. "Half the cumin now, the way it says, and half stirred in at the end. Then we taste both."

"Science," Theodore said solemnly, "with curry." He held out a spoon as if knighting her.

The seeds hit the ghee and within seconds the smell changed, warm and toasty and suddenly everywhere, like the pan had woken up. Freyja leaned over from her station. "My gran calls that tadka," she said. "Frying the whole spices in hot oil first." Anna filed the word away and kept going, because the onions were not going to wait for anyone's grandmother.

The flatbread was its own small crisis. The dough stuck to the rolling pin, then to itself, and Anna remembered her mother telling her to let dough rest and Anna, impatient at nine years old, refusing. She had pounded out flatbreads that came out like shields. This time she covered the dough with a cloth and let it rest while the curry simmered, and when she rolled it, it moved like it wanted to cooperate.

The timing nearly collapsed anyway. The rice finished early, the curry needed five more minutes, and Anna negotiated with the clock by wrapping the pot in two tea towels to hold its heat, a trick she'd seen Ms. Henry use without ever being told it was allowed. The flatbreads puffed in the pan, one after another, and then everything landed on the counter in the same minute: rice, curry, three warm breads.

The tasting was the real test. Anna took two spoons of curry, the tadka batch and the late-cumin batch, and did not say which was which. Theodore chewed the first spoonful, then the second, then went back to the first like a man returning to a good room. "This one," he said. "The other one tastes like... cumin that never got the message."

Anna tasted it herself. The seeds stirred in at the end were sharp and a little raw, standing apart from everything, while the fried ones had melted into the whole dish, the flavour riding through the ghee into the onions and the sauce. So the fat had to come first. The pan had to teach the spices before anything else joined them.

"What's the word again?" Theodore asked, already reaching for the last flatbread.

"Tadka," Freyja said, and Anna got there half a second behind her, both of them saying it at once, and Freyja laughed so hard she nearly dropped the curry spoon.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen every two hours outdoors, and immediately after swimming or sweating.
story:
The ferry's engines hummed under Jasmine's sneakers as she leaned on the rail, watching the mainland shrink to a brown smudge. Delaney stood beside her, and Lamar had claimed a bench where he was attempting to photograph a seagull that refused to cooperate. "Beach day," Delaney said, holding up a bottle. "My mom works for a corporation that makes sunscreen, so we get it free. I have six bottles." Jasmine had put on sunscreen that morning at the house, before the long drive to the dock. She figured she was set.

Their neighbor Ms. Tan was on the ferry too, knitting in the shade of the cabin. "You two are going to roast out there," she said, not looking up from her needles. "Sunscreen doesn't last all day, you know." Jasmine nodded politely and didn't believe her. How could something you put on at nine in the morning just quit? It was still on her skin, faintly coconut-scented. It must still be working.

They hit the beach before noon. Jasmine checked her phone at eleven, at twelve, at one, and did the math: two hours had passed, then more. She was proud of herself for noticing, in a distant, filing-it-away sort of way. Then she and Delaney and Lamar spent the rest of the afternoon in and out of the waves, racing to the buoy, dragging each other off the paddleboard, towel-drying, going back in. Nobody reapplied anything. Lamar said the water would preserve whatever protection remained, like wax on a car, and that sounded scientific enough that nobody argued.

That evening, back on the ferry for the return trip, Jasmine's shoulders began to sting. By the time the lights of the harbor appeared, they were the color of the boiled ham her grandmother made, a distinct, glowing pink that hurt when her jacket brushed it. Delaney's nose had peeled already, a little white flap like a price sticker. Lamar, mysteriously, was fine, and he would not stop mentioning it.

Jasmine sat down across from Ms. Tan, who took one look and raised her eyebrows over her knitting. "It wears off," Jasmine said slowly, working it through. "It doesn't last the whole day. You have to put it on again every two hours out there. And right after swimming, or sweating, not later. Right after." She counted backward on her fingers: morning application, hours of sun, hours of waves. The whole afternoon had been one long expiration notice she hadn't read.

"You could have told me straight out," she added. Ms. Tan snipped her yarn. "I did, dear. Twice." Delaney appeared with one of her six bottles and set it solemnly in Jasmine's hands. "For tomorrow," she said. "We leave at nine. I'll set an alarm." Lamar leaned over the rail and shouted, "Two hours!" at the seagull, which, for once, did not argue.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
story:
Mia spread her survey papers across the workbench in the garage, weighting the corners with wrenches so the fan in the window wouldn't scatter them. Fifty kids had answered her two questions: did you eat breakfast this morning, and what did you get on the last math quiz? Her poster was due Friday, and Mr. Wright had already warned her that a science fair project needed more than a pretty chart. She'd been meticulous about the data, checking every name against every number twice, and the pattern was clear. Kids who ate breakfast scored higher. Almost every time.

"So breakfast makes you smarter," said Jayden, who had biked over to help her glue the title letters. He held up a B and squinted at it. "Done. Can we eat now?"

"It's not done." Mia tapped the graph with her pencil. "What if breakfast isn't the thing doing it?"

Jayden stuck the B on crooked, then peeled it off again. "What else would it be? The cereal has, like, magic vitamins?"

That was the problem. Mia kept thinking about last year, when she'd blamed her dying pepper plant on the new fertilizer and switched back to the old one, and the pepper had died anyway. It turned out the neighbor's tree had grown in and shaded the whole pot. Two things had changed together, the fertilizer and the shade, and she'd picked the wrong one to blame. She had spent a whole month being wrong, and she still felt the sting of it when she thought about how sure she'd been.

"Here's my test," she said, pulling a fresh sheet toward her. "Zack's in the car pool with kids from three different streets. He knows everybody's mornings." She wrote Zack's name at the top and a third question below the first two: what time do your parents make you go to bed on school nights? Then she called him, and he shouted the answers down the line while she filled in rows, because Zack knew everyone's bedtimes the way other kids knew video game scores.

When she plotted it, the twist showed up in blue dots. The breakfast kids were almost all the early-bedtime kids. The ones who skipped cereal were the ones up past ten, rushing out the door with a granola bar. Something behind both, the parents or the sleep or the whole schedule, might be causing breakfast and the quiz scores both.

"Jayden," she said slowly, "the numbers going up and down together. That's called correlation." She underlined her new poster heading: CORRELATION IS NOT CAUSE. She couldn't yet say what the hidden factor was, and maybe she never could, and that unanswered part itched.

Jayden studied the blue dots for a long moment. "So your poster says you were wrong?"

"It says I found out what I don't know yet." Mia picked up the glue stick. "Hold the C straight this time."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
Zack stood in the gym holding one end of a banner that said ARMENIAN DIASPORA CLUB in tall blue letters. The family cultural festival had taken over the whole school, and his aunt had dragged him along because, she said, everyone should bring something. Arman's table was near the door, and Arman had grabbed Zack the moment he walked in, saying he needed someone tall to hold the other side while he taped the top edge.

"Perfect," Arman said, stepping back to check the banner. Behind the table sat his grandmother and two uncles, all of them ladling out rice and talking over each other in a mix of Armenian and English. The gym smelled like butter, burnt coffee and floor wax. A woman stopped, squinted at the banner, and asked what "diaspora" meant. Arman opened his mouth, then closed it. One uncle said it was a kind of dance. The grandmother said it was a town in the old country. The woman thanked them and moved on, looking unconvinced, and Zack could tell she thought the club had made up its own word.

The problem nagged at him while he helped stack paper cups. Arman was embarrassed; his whole table looked smaller now, somehow diminished, because the one word on their banner was a mystery even to them. Zack reasoned that a word people put on a banner must be a real word, and real words had meanings that somebody knew. He scanned the gym. Mr. Ricci, the librarian, was working the Italian table, and librarians knew words the way the coach knew plays. Zack left Presley guarding the cups and walked over, past a desolate little table with no one behind it and a sad bowl of crackers.

Mr. Ricci didn't just tell him. He handed Zack the festival program and pointed at the language section. "Try the Greek," he said, which was a strange thing to say about a program printed in English, until Zack flipped it over and found a tiny glossary in the back, between the map and the thank-you list. He read the entry twice, then a third time, mouthing it.

He walked back fast. "Diaspora," he said to Arman, holding up the program. "It comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors." Arman read it himself, then laughed and called his grandmother over, pointing at the page. She read it, nodded slowly, and said something in Armenian to the uncles, who both went quiet, then started talking at once.

The woman came back around, this time with two friends. "So what does your banner mean?" she asked. Arman straightened up and repeated the line word for word, then added, "My family's from three different countries, and before that, all from one place." He waved at the map hanging behind the table, little pins stuck across half the globe. One of the friends asked where the pins were now, and Arman handed her a pin and pointed at the map.

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: Two triangles are congruent when they have exactly the same shape and size, so all three pairs of matching sides and all three pairs of matching angles are equal.
story:
Caleb slid the last triangle tile across the table and frowned at it. Ms. Sadeghi had set out cardboard triangles for the community centre math club challenge: figure out which triangles matched, using only a ruler and a protractor, no stacking allowed. "Two triangles are congruent when they have exactly the same shape and size," she had said, "so all three pairs of matching sides and all three pairs of matching angles are equal." Caleb had written that in his notebook, but now he stared at triangles C and F and wondered how he could possibly check six things with the clock running out.

"Could we just measure everything?" Leon asked, flipping his ruler over. "Three sides and three angles each. That's twelve measurements for one pair."

"That takes forever," Maelie said, already measuring anyway. "And my protractor keeps slipping."

Caleb picked up triangles C and F and held them side by side against the window light. The afternoon sun made the cardboard almost transparent, and he could see the edges of one through the other. They looked like the same shape, but looks weren't proof. He measured two sides of triangle C, then the angle squeezed between them, then the same spots on triangle F. Same. Same. Same. His pencil hovered. If two sides and the angle between them matched, did the rest have to match too? It was like a door with two hinges, he thought. Once those were fixed, the far corner couldn't wander off anywhere else.

"Try it on another pair," Maelie said, watching him. "If it works twice, maybe it's a real rule and not luck."

They tested triangles A and D the same way, two sides and the squeezed angle, and when they measured the leftover parts afterward, every remaining side and angle came out equal too. Leon, who had insisted from the start that they'd need all six pairs, set down his ruler. "Okay," he said slowly, "I change my mind. You don't need to check everything. Half the triangle drags the other half along."

Ms. Sadeghi walked past their table, and Caleb held up his notebook. "We only measured two sides and the angle between them, and the triangles still matched perfectly. Is that a real rule?"

"That's called the side-angle-side rule," she said, and kept walking, which meant yes, figure out the rest.

On the bus home, Caleb kept thinking about the hidden chain inside it, the logic of one fixed angle pulling two fixed sides together until the third corner had nowhere else to go. At home he cut two more triangles out of cereal box cardboard, careful with the scissors, and stacked them on the kitchen table. His little sister leaned over his shoulder. He pressed the top one down flat. Every edge lined up, corner for corner, not a sliver of the bottom one showing anywhere.

"See?" he said. "Same shape, same size. Congruent." He tapped the matched edges. "Now watch what happens when I make one angle different."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers aged 13 to 18.
story:
Alexia kept a tally sheet taped inside her footlocker, and by Thursday night she had filled four rows of it. Every time her hands went cold and her stomach knotted, she made a check mark and wrote the hour. The checks clustered between nine and ten in the morning, right before canoe practice, and again after lights-out when she lay listening to the loons. What she wanted to know was why. Stress was supposed to have a cause, like a test or a bear, and neither one was waiting for her at the end of the dock.

On Friday, Ms. Oyelaran, the water-safety instructor, gathered the swimmers on the porch before the morning lesson. "When you capsize, you panic and breathe like a startled cat," she said. "Watch me demonstrate what to do instead." She drew a square in the air with her finger, breathing in for four counts, holding, breathing out for four, holding again. Alexia copied her, and the tight band around her ribs loosened a little. Interesting, she thought. So the breathing could be steered, like a canoe. But a square breath in the morning didn't explain why the knots arrived in the first place.

That night she added a second column to her tally sheet: hours of sleep. Camp lights-out was ten, and reveille blew at seven, which was nine hours if she actually slept. But she didn't. The loons, the heat, the scratchy wool blanket, and, lately, a strange tapping sound from the direction of the boathouse kept her up past midnight most nights. She did the subtraction twice because she didn't believe it. Five hours, maybe six. At home she slept until ten on weekends. Could the missing hours be the hidden cause, and the cold hands only the signal?

She decided to test it. Saturday she skipped the campfire, did Ms. Oyelaran's square breathing in her bunk until her eyelids dropped, and counted ten slow breaths every time she woke. Nine hours, by her estimate. Sunday morning she felt like a different person, and her tally sheet held only one check mark, before canoes, where it belonged.

Then came the twist. Sunday after breakfast, Erik wandered over, yawning so wide she could count his fillings. He was playing the emperor in the cabin skit that afternoon, and he'd been rehearsing lines at midnight, he admitted, along with something else. "There's an old gaming console in the boathouse. That tapping you heard? Gabriel's the one sneaking out to use it." Gabriel, who was twelve, looked sheepish. "I stay up till about midnight playing," he said. "Then I'm up at seven."

Alexia grabbed a stick and wrote in the dirt. "How much is that, midnight to seven?" Gabriel counted on his fingers. "Seven hours, I guess. Sounds like plenty." She shook her head and pulled the camp handbook from her back pocket, open to the page she'd found in the infirmary while waiting for her blister kit. It said the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers aged 13 to 18. Gabriel stared at the numbers. "I'm twelve. I need at least nine. I'm two short, every single night." He thought about his short temper all week, how it had crept through the cabin like something corrosive eating away at everyone's good mood, and how Erik kept falling asleep mid-rehearsal. "The emperor needs his rest too," Erik said, and Gabriel handed the console's power cord to Alexia for safekeeping until checkout day.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Clay pieces must be completely dry before they are fired in a kiln, because leftover water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece.
story:
Logan had exactly two days to finish the clay bowl he was making for his grandmother's birthday, and the kiln in her garage only fired on Friday nights because that was when his grandfather ran it. The bowl was for a surprise gift, and the surprise would be ruined if Grandma found it half-finished on her own kitchen table, so Logan had smuggled it down to the garage in a shoebox and set it on the shelf beside the kiln.

Cash and Harleen came over after school to help him carve the rim. "You should put waves all the way around," Harleen said, tracing a finger in the air. "Then it keeps its symmetry, no matter which way she turns it." Logan liked that idea, so the three of them pressed small scallops into the clay until the whole circle matched, even the tricky part near the handle where his thumb kept slipping. When they finished, the bowl looked like something a real potter might have made, and Logan carried it back to the shelf feeling taller than he had that morning.

That was when he noticed something odd. The little hedgehog figurine he had made last week sat in a pile of dust and cracks, split nearly in two, its snout broken clean off. He picked up the pieces and turned them over. He had fired it himself on Friday, following Grandpa's checklist, and it had come out of the kiln already broken. Nobody had dropped it. Nothing had fallen on it. He set the pieces in his palm and stared at them, wondering what could break something inside a hot kiln where nothing could touch it.

"I have to confess something," Cash said, watching him. "When you loaded it, you were in a hurry. I saw you put it in straight from the windowsill." Logan frowned. The windowsill, where the hedgehog had sat overnight. He walked over and touched the sill, then touched the bowl on the shelf, then touched the sill again. The sill was warm from the sun. The bowl felt cool, the kind of cool that lingers in a basement corner. He remembered that the hedgehog had felt cool too, that same coolness, when he carried it to the kiln.

"Wait," Harleen said slowly. "My mom's mugs. When they came out of the dishwasher still warm, the cool spots meant they were still wet somewhere." Logan held the bowl against his wrist, where skin is most vulnerable to cold, and the chill pressed back at him like a damp cloth. The bowl was still holding water somewhere inside, invisible, deep in the clay. He thought about the hedgehog: sealed inside a hot kiln, and its hidden water had nowhere to go. He didn't know exactly how it had burst the clay apart, but he knew it had.

So he moved the bowl off the shelf and set it on the warm sill where the hedgehog had sat, right in the stripe of afternoon sun. "It has to be completely dry before it goes in the kiln," he told Cash. "All the way dry. Leftover water turns to steam, and steam can crack it or burst it." Cash nodded and helped him turn the bowl a quarter turn every hour so no side stayed damp and hidden.

By Friday the bowl felt warm all the way through, no coolness anywhere, and it rang faintly when Logan tapped it with a knuckle, a sound the hedgehog had never made. Grandpa looked it over, then looked at the broken pieces Logan had lined up on the bench, and gave him a small nod. That night they loaded the kiln together, the bowl sitting tall on the top shelf, and Grandpa shut the heavy door and turned the dial.

At the birthday party on Sunday, Grandma lifted the bowl out of its wrapping and turned it slowly, watching the waves run around the rim. "It's perfect," she said, and Logan grinned at Cash across the table.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
The Regional tryout was still four days away, and Tristan had already chewed three pencils down to splinters. He sat at the kitchen table staring at the scholarship flyer, the one with the tropical beach printed behind the words, as though a coach from some warm place might appear and pluck him off this rainy street. Leena was across from him, watching him shred a fourth pencil.

"You did this before regionals last year," she said. "You didn't sleep for a week, and then you were fine on the day."

"I wasn't fine. My hands shook the whole first half." Tristan flipped the pencil over and chewed the other end. "But that's the thing. On the day it's different. On the day there's an actual ball, an actual keeper bearing down on me. Right now there's nothing. Nothing has happened yet, and I feel worse."

Leena tilted her head. "So when the keeper's actually coming at you, that's one thing. And this," she waved at the pencils, the flyer, him, "is another thing entirely?"

Ms. Cho, his neighbour, had said something like that once, and Tristan tried to remember it while stacking his mangled pencils into a tower. She'd been talking about her own son before a big exam. She had used a word for it, and it had stuck with him because it sounded like a made-up word at the time. He closed his eyes, and it came back. He'd thought she was just being reassuring, the way adults are, but maybe she'd been describing an actual difference. He tested it out loud.

"Fear is when the threat is happening right now," he said. "Anxiety is when the threat might happen later. So the keeper is fear, and this week is anxiety." He opened his eyes. "That means I've been fighting the wrong thing. I've been trying to make my hands stop shaking for a game that doesn't exist yet."

He got up, found a notebook, and wrote two columns: NOW and MAYBE LATER. Under NOW he put nothing, because no keeper had burst through the kitchen door. Under MAYBE LATER he wrote tryout, missed shot, coach's face. He had to integrate the two lists somehow, but not by pretending they were the same list. His mother had a rule about screens after nine, and he'd always thought it was arbitrary, but now he thought maybe rules were like that: a wall you build before the flood, a boundary you draw while you're calm.

For the next three days he ran the drill at the park each afternoon, and each evening he crossed one thing off the MAYBE LATER column, because a worry you name, he'd discovered, is smaller than a worry you don't. On the morning of the tryout, when the keeper actually did bear down on him, his hands shook exactly like last year, and he scored anyway.

Afterward, mud to the knees, he found Leena on the sideline and held up his notebook, which had somehow survived in his bag.

"NOW," he said. "Everything in that column, one time only."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
story:
Arthur arrived at the pool with his goggles fogged from the walk over, which he took as a bad sign. He wiped them on his shirt and counted the lanes. Six lanes, forty kids, one clipboard-carrying coach, and about four minutes of water time per swimmer. If he wanted the last spot on the school swim team, he would have to make those four minutes count.

Then he noticed Brianna standing at the shallow end, twisting her cap in her hands. "I thought girls' tryouts were Thursday," he said. She shook her head. "There is no girls' team. There's only one team, and the notice said boys' swim tryouts." She looked at the water like it was a locked door. "So I'm just going to get in lane four and swim, and see what happens."

Arthur wondered about that. Not about Brianna swimming; she was fast, faster than him off the blocks, though he'd never say so out loud because his pride had a tender spot somewhere near the cartilage of his ego. What he wondered about was the sign. His school got federal money, he was pretty sure, because the envelope from the district office last fall had a sentence about federal funding in it, and his mom had squinted at it over her nutritious lentil soup and muttered something about paperwork. If a school took that money, was it allowed to print "boys" on a sports notice and leave it there? He had a feeling it wasn't, the same feeling he got when a math answer came out to fourteen and something in him whispered, check that again.

He couldn't see the rule itself, so he did what he always did with invisible things: he tested it. While the coach barked "Flutter kicks, go!" Arthur swam over and asked, as casually as a boy in chlorine-shocked goggles can ask anything, "Does our school take federal money?" The coach squinted. "Every public school does. Why?"

"Because my social studies teacher, Ms. Hughes, had a poster about it," Arthur said. "Title IX. It's a law from 1972, and it bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. It covers sports too." He held his breath. The coach looked at Brianna, then at the clipboard, then made a face like a man realizing his shoelaces had been tied together all morning.

"Well," the coach said, "let me clarify my paperwork before I need a lawyer instead of a whistle." He scratched out "boys'" with his pen, wrote "swim team tryouts, all students," and bellowed, "Lane four, you're up!" Brianna snapped her cap on and grinned at Arthur.

During the two-hundred free, Arthur discovered that watching Brianna swim was like watching weather happen, and that his own chances of making the team had possibly just sunk below the diving ring he'd lost in fourth grade. When they both climbed out, dripping and gasping, the coach walked over with the clipboard tucked under his arm. "Pryce, Okafor," he said. "Times were close. Tell you what. You two race again Monday, and the loser carries the kickboard bin all season." Brianna stuck out a wet hand. "Deal," she said, and Arthur shook it, already plotting to eat something nutritious and secretly nutritious for him too, all weekend.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture.
story:
Elliot sat at the lunch table with his phone out, making a group chat for the geography project. He typed, "Team: me, Cedar, Bryn," and added the two of them. Cedar was already across from him, eating fries. Bryn was new, three weeks into the term, and had said yes so fast when Elliot asked him to join that Elliot felt a little proud of himself.

The project was to make a map page for each person in the group: a photo, a flag, and three facts about where you were from. Elliot wrote in the chat, "I'll do Canada. Cedar, you're doing Greece, right?" Cedar thumbed a thumbs-up. Then Elliot typed, "Bryn, which country do you want?" He watched Bryn's phone light up across the cafeteria. Bryn read it, put the phone face down, and didn't answer.

At recess Elliot tried in person. "So which flag do you want for your page? I can grab you a printer pass if you need one." Bryn kicked at the edge of the soccer pitch. "It's not that easy." "How is it not easy? Everyone's from somewhere." "I've lived in Singapore, then Germany, then Brazil, then here. Four countries. My dad's British and my mom's Filipino, and my grandparents' house is in London, and I've been there, like, twice." He shrugged. "People ask where I'm from and I just resent the question. It's like there's one right answer and I always get it wrong." Then he went to line up for the ball and the conversation was over.

Elliot told Cedar about it under the oak tree. "Maybe it's not a country," Cedar said. "Maybe it's a group." That was the idea Elliot wanted to test: a group with a name, the way "only children" or "left-handers" was a group with a name. He searched on his phone, scrolling past the tedious first pages of ads and a forum about moving companies, until he found a page from a sociology site. He read it twice, then read a line out loud. "Says here an American sociologist, Ruth Hill Useem, coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s." "What's it mean?" Cedar asked. "Kids raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture," Elliot said, still reading.

That afternoon in Mr. Lau's room, before the bell, Elliot typed into the group chat: "Question. Is four countries part of a thing called third culture kid? Asking for the map page." He hit send before he could change his mind. Three dots appeared, then stopped, then appeared again. Bryn replied with a single word: "Maybe." Then, a minute later: "Come to the library and I'll show you my list."

Elliot and Cedar found Bryn at the corner table with a notebook open. Across the top of the page he had written "THIRD CULTURE KID" in block letters, and underneath, four columns for four countries, each one full of foods and words and friends' names. He slid it toward them. "For the map page. We might need a bigger flag section."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
story:
Ariana found the anthology in the back corner of the bookshop, between a shelf of cookbooks and a display rack standing almost perpendicular to the wall. Mr. Brennan, the owner, let her class sit in that corner on Saturdays, and today Skyler and Billy had come along, because on Monday they would have to explain the ending of the story they had all finished on Friday.

"I still don't get it," Billy said, dropping onto the rug. "We read the whole thing and nobody saw it coming. That's not fair. Teachers always say a good story warns you."

Skyler flipped to the first page. "It starts so calm. Kids running around, flowers, summer."

Ariana leaned over her shoulder. The first paragraph said the morning was clear and sunny, that school had just let out, and that the boys were making a great pile of stones in one corner of the square while the girls stood aside talking. When she had first read it, she had skipped right past the stones. They had seemed like nothing, just kids playing. Now the words sat differently on the page, the way a straight line looks crooked after you learn it was drawn next to a perpendicular one.

"Go back to the stones," she said slowly. Skyler read the sentence aloud. Ariana made her read it again, and a third time, and Billy groaned, but she kept her finger on the line. The story had appeared in The New Yorker back in 1948, Mr. Brennan had told them, and people had written angry letters because it blindsided them. But it hadn't, not really. The stones were there in the very first paragraph, quietly piling up while everyone was busy noticing the sunshine.

"Wait," Skyler whispered. "They collect the stones at the start. And at the end..." She didn't finish, and Ariana didn't want her to, not out loud, not yet.

"Try it," Ariana said. "Cover everything except this first paragraph. Read it like it's the whole story." Billy did, frowning, mouthing the words. His frown deepened. Then his head came up.

"The kids are gathering rocks," he said. "In a nice little town. On a nice little day." He swallowed. "Ariana, why would kids gather rocks unless somebody was going to throw them?"

Ariana pulled out her notebook and wrote the story's title, Shirley Jackson's The Lottery, at the top of a fresh page. Her hand was shaking a little, and she noticed that Skyler's was too. Under the title she wrote one word, and turned the notebook so they both could see it: foreshadowing.

"That's what we tell the class on Monday," she said. "The warning was there the whole time."

"Buying that book now would be an expense," Mr. Brennan called from the register, and Billy laughed, a little shakily, and walked over with the anthology in both hands.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
Edouard had made the county spelling bee twice, and both times he had gone out in round three. The bee was held in the public library on Front Street, in the big room with the mural of a sailing ship, and this Saturday it was mandatory for spellers to check in by one o'clock sharp. He had five days left.

His method had always been the same: reread the word list until his eyes ached. On Monday night his mother sat down across from him and closed his notebook. "You've read that page six times," she said. "Close the book. I'll say the words, you spell them out loud."

He got "chalet" wrong, and "bivouac" wrong, and "gelatinous" wrong, all words he was sure he had stared at. That stung, but it also gave him an idea. Rereading felt smooth and safe. Being quizzed felt rough, and the rough words were the ones he missed. Maybe the roughness was the point. He asked his mother to keep the book and quiz him every night, and he started writing each misspelled word in a red notebook.

At school on Wednesday he told Gwyneth and Jaiden about it. "There's a study about this," Gwyneth said. She looked it up on the library computer during their free period. "Two researchers, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke. In 2006 they found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it." Jaiden frowned and said he would stick to rereading, because reading was how you learned things. "You're competing too," Edouard said. "Test it on yourself tonight. One night. If it doesn't work, go back."

By Friday, Edouard's red notebook had shrunk to a dozen words, and "bivouac" was not one of them. Jaiden cornered him in the hallway. "I tried it," Jaiden said. "My sister quizzed me. I'm not reading that list again. My mom tried to enforce reading time and I told her no." Edouard's mother had offered to call a colleague from work who had been a speller, but Edouard had said the quiz was enough.

Saturday, one o'clock, the mural room. Thirty-one spellers stood in a line. Round three arrived like it always did, and the pronouncer said, "Bivouac." Edouard asked for the language of origin, asked for it in a sentence, then spelled it without a single doubt. Jaiden, four spellers later, nailed "gelatinous" and grinned down the line at Edouard.

They were both still standing in round six when the pronouncer said, "Your word is colleagues."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and old sweat, and the jerseys were anonymous, numbered but nameless, which Jaxson decided was the point. Nobody cared who you were until you made the team. He stood in line with twenty other sixth graders waiting for basketball tryouts to start, bouncing on his toes, feeling fast.

Zak did not look fast. Zak looked like a guy who had run to catch a bus and then the bus had backed over him. His dribbles in the warm-up line went halfway up his shin. When he missed a layup so badly that it hit the bottom of the backboard, Jaxson pulled him aside by the water bottles.

"How late did you stay up?"

Zak stared at the floor. "Two."

"Two in the morning? Doing what?"

"New game came out." Zak wouldn't quite confess to more than that, but his face did. "I figured I'd be fine. I slept till seven. That's like five hours."

Last month flashed through Jaxson's mind: the science unit on health, the chart Ms. Boateng had pinned to the wall. He'd copied it into his notebook because she said it might be on the quiz, and he'd read it again that night mostly because his phone was dead. U.S. sleep experts recommend nine to twelve hours a night for kids aged six to twelve, and eight to ten for teenagers. Five was nowhere on the chart. Five wasn't even close to the teenage end, and they weren't even teenagers yet.

He tested his theory out loud. "You're twelve, right? So you needed nine to twelve hours last night. Minimum. You got five."

"So I'm seven hours short," Zak said, doing the math with the doomed expression of a man tallying a bill.

"That's a whole night's sleep for a little kid, almost."

They didn't have time to fix it, but Jaxson had a simple idea anyway. "Stop chasing the ball. Stand where the ball comes to you, and pass. You can still look smart without running." It worked about as well as anything could work. Zak planted himself near the free-throw line like a lamppost, and twice the ball came to him and twice he fired clean passes to open players. The coach, a tall woman with a whistle and a clipboard, wrote something down both times. During a water break she held up a ball and told them to take care of the equipment because it cost real money, some composite polymer shell that cracked if you left it in the cold, which was more science than anyone expected at tryouts.

At the end she read the numbers of the twelve who made the first cut. Jaxson's number was third. Zak's was last, announced almost as an afterthought, and Zak grinned like it had been read first.

"Survival by passing," Zak said. "Tomorrow I'm sleeping ten hours. Ten's inside the nine-to-twelve."

"Tomorrow you could sleep twelve and still pass like a lamppost," Jaxson said, and tossed him the ball.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The saying that compound interest is 'the eighth wonder of the world' is often credited to Albert Einstein, but there is no reliable evidence he ever said it.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen table was covered with graph paper, a calculator, and a tin of lemon drops, because Blake's presentation for Ms. Haddad's class was due tomorrow morning and he still could not explain the difference between simple and compound interest in a way anyone would remember. He had started with five cents in the title and it had gone downhill from there.

"Read me your opening line," Grandpa said, sliding the lemon drops closer.

Blake held up his notecard. "Albert Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world."

Grandpa popped a lemon drop in his mouth and chewed slowly, which Blake had learned was a bad sign. "Where'd you find that?"

"On the internet. Three different websites." Blake flipped through his notecards. "It's a great hook. Ms. Haddad loves hooks."

"Three websites copying each other isn't a source, it's a rumor with a stamp on it." Grandpa pulled the laptop across the table. "You've got until Joyce and Connie get here at four to practice, so let's check it."

They checked. Blake typed "Einstein compound interest quote" into a search, and the first thing that came up was a fact-checking article. He read it twice, and his stomach dropped a little, the way it did when the warranty on his bike turned out not to cover the bent wheel after all. The quote was often credited to Einstein, but there was no reliable evidence he ever said it.

"So I can't use it," Blake said.

"You could say that, though. That it's often credited to him but there's no proof. That's actually a better hook, because now you're the kid who checked." Grandpa tapped the graph paper. "Meanwhile, you still haven't shown the difference between simple and compound. Five years, right?"

Blake grabbed the calculator. With simple interest, the bank paid you the same amount every year, flat, like a straight line. With compound, the interest earned its own interest, and the line bent upward. He could see it in the numbers, but he could not see why it mattered, not really, until he drew the two lines on the same graph and watched the gap between them widen year after year like a slowly opening door.

The doorbell rang at four exactly. Joyce carried a poster board, and Connie carried her tablet with the timer already running, because they had promised Ms. Haddad they would rehearse twice before dinner.

"Did you fix the Einstein thing?" Joyce asked, setting down the poster. "Connie and I argued about it on the way over."

Connie held up her tablet. "I looked it up during walk. Same thing. Often credited to him, no reliable evidence he said it. Sorry, Blake."

Blake lined up his notecards and took a breath. "That's the good news. Watch this."

He drew two lines in the air with his finger, one flat, one climbing, and started his presentation from the top.

"Open with the rumor," Connie said, starting the timer. "Then hit them with the graph."

"Three minutes," Joyce counted. "Go."

Blake flipped the first card. "Everybody says Albert Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. Here's the thing: nobody can prove he said it."

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: A qualifier is a word such as 'usually', 'most' or 'probably' that limits how strongly a claim is stated, making it harder to disprove.
story:
The auditorium smelled like dust and old velvet, and the stage lights made everything look yellow. Isaac sat in the third row with his debate notebook open, trying to build his first real case for Saturday's tournament. Mr. Cho had written three words on the whiteboard: claim, evidence, warrant. Isaac understood the first two, sort of, but the third one kept slipping away from him like water.

"Your turn," Mr. Cho said. "Give me a claim about homework."

Isaac stood. "All kids hate homework."

Yassin, two rows back, raised his hand without waiting. "My cousin Priya loves homework. She does extra problems on weekends. So that claim is wrong, and I didn't even need evidence to knock it down."

The whole row laughed, and Isaac felt his confidence start to evaporate. One counterexample. That was all it had taken.

"Try again," said Mr. Cho. "Same idea, different words."

Isaac stared at his notebook. He thought about how his own sister grumbled every night, and how Presley complained constantly, and how he himself groaned whenever the teacher assigned a chapter of questions. But then he thought about Priya, out there somewhere doing math for fun, and about kids he didn't even know. He couldn't see all the kids in the world, so he couldn't prove anything about all of them. But a pattern was still a pattern, even with holes in it. He crossed out "all" and wrote something new.

"Most kids dislike homework," he said. "A survey in our textbook says seventy percent of middle schoolers report stress about homework. That's my evidence. And the warrant is that if seventy percent report stress, then most of them dislike the thing causing it." He looked at Yassin. "Go ahead. Find me a kid who loves it."

Yassin grinned. "Priya still loves it. But one Priya doesn't beat seventy percent. You win this one."

Mr. Cho tapped the whiteboard. "What Isaac just did has a name. A qualifier. Usually, most, probably, words like that."

Isaac wrote the word down and underlined it twice. It felt strange, like admitting weakness made his case stronger instead of weaker. He looked at his notes for Saturday and began fixing every claim that said "always" or "never."

For practice, Presley stood and argued that owls sleep through every daylight hour, and Isaac caught it right away. "Owls are nocturnal, but 'every' is a stretch. Say usually." Then Presley argued that lichen grows on every rock in the creek behind the school, and Isaac shook his head before she even finished.

"You're getting it," Mr. Cho said, checking the clock. "Same time tomorrow. Bring three claims, each one with its qualifier."

Isaac packed his notebook slowly, reading the underlined word one more time. Then he jogged up the aisle after Presley and Yassin, already arguing about whether most people actually like pizza, or only probably.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A slow leak can be found by pumping some air into the tube and holding it under water to watch for bubbles.
story:
Sophia knelt beside her bike in the rack outside Martelli's Grocery, where the front tyre had gone soft as a day-old balloon sometime between breakfast and now. Noor crouched next to her, holding the repair kit they had pooled their allowance to buy.

"We have forty minutes before the ride to the lake starts," Noor said, checking her phone. "If we're late, Sophie's mom leaves without us."

Sophia flipped the bike upside down on its handlebars, the way she had seen racers do, and spun the wheel. The tyre had no gash, no nail, no thorn sticking out of it. That was the bizarre part. A flat should look flat, hurt somewhere you could see, but this one was hiding its wound like it wanted to evade her completely.

Her grandfather had shown her what to do about holes that hide, back in his garage last summer. She could still see the rusted bucket, the clear water, the old tube he had pumped a little air into. "Watch," he had said, and lowered the tube beneath the surface. After a moment a thin string of bubbles rose from one spot, quick and silver, like the tube was whispering its secret. Find the bubbles, find the hole. That was all there was to it.

"I need a bucket," Sophia said now. "And water."

"Where are you getting a bucket at a grocery store?"

Sophia stood and pushed through the doors into the cool, bright aisles. In produce, Ms. Wu, the manager who lived on her street and always saved the bruised apples for the food shelf, was stacking melons. Sophia explained the flat, the deadline, the bucket. Ms. Wu didn't laugh or sigh at her.

"There's a mop bucket in the back," she said, "and a tap. Bring it back when you're done." She handed Sophia the key on a wooden spoon. When Noor mouthed a thank-you, Ms. Wu only said, "I rode everywhere at your age. Flats and I are old friends."

Outside, Sophia wedged the tyre levers under the bead of the tyre, working them around the rim the way her grandfather's hands had, until the tube came free, wrinkled and pale. She pumped some air into it until it fattened up, then pushed the whole thing under the water in the mop bucket. At first, nothing. Noor leaned in beside her, both of them staring at the still surface.

"There," Noor whispered.

A thread of bubbles rose from a spot near the valve, one bubble after another, tiny and stubborn. Sophia marked it with the wax crayon from the kit, dried the tube, roughed the spot with the sandpaper, and pressed on the patch while Noor counted to sixty out loud. When she pumped the tyre back to firm and it held, they both felt like shouting.

They returned the bucket, and Ms. Wu checked the tyre with a squeeze of her hand. "Better than new," she said.

Sophia wheeled the bike toward the lake path, Noor jogging beside her, and called over her shoulder, "See you at the food shelf on Saturday!"

"Bring the bike," Ms. Wu called back. "I've got a bucket with your name on it."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
story:
Aubrey had never done a load of laundry in her life, and Grandma had decided that today was the day to fix that. "You sort, you wash, you fold," Grandma said, setting a basket of clothes on the utility room floor. "I'll be in the garden if you get stuck."

Aubrey dumped the basket out and began making piles: dark jeans and a navy sweater in one, towels and socks in another, a white tablecloth by itself. She was reaching for the detergent shelf when her friend Faye knocked on the back door, holding the science homework they were supposed to do together. "You're doing laundry?" Faye said. "My mom just does mine."

"Grandma says the cumulative effect of never learning anything is that you grow up helpless," Aubrey said. "Her exact words. Come help me anyway. You can read the bottles while I figure out the machine." The tablecloth had a stain, a brown smear right in the middle, and Aubrey remembered Grandma once saying bleach took out stains on whites. She found a bottle marked chlorine bleach and carried it toward the sink, where a bucket of soapy water already sat waiting from the morning's floor scrubbing.

Faye was reading labels out loud, the way she read everything. "Chlorine bleach. Hmm. This other one says it's an ammonia cleaner." She looked at the bucket, then at the bottle in Aubrey's hand. "Wait. Both of those are going in the same water?"

Aubrey stopped with the bottle tilted over the bucket. She hadn't thought about it. She read the fine print on the bleach label herself, the tiny warning print that most people probably never read at all. "It says never mix with cleaners containing ammonia," she said slowly. "Together they release chloramine. That's a toxic gas."

"A gas? From two liquids?" Faye leaned in, not too close. "That's like an invisible reaction. You can't see it happening until it's too late."

Aubrey set the bleach on the shelf, well away from the bucket, and thought about last summer, when she'd mixed fizzy drink and milk on a dare just to see what happened. Nothing had happened, and she'd laughed. This was different, and she couldn't have said exactly how she knew it was, except that the label was not joking around. She emptied the bucket down the drain, rinsed it twice, and filled it fresh with plain water for the tablecloth alone.

Later, when the load had gone through and the tablecloth came out clean and the whole utility room smelled of nothing worse than detergent, Grandma came inside and found the two girls folding towels. Aubrey told her about the labels. Grandma nodded. "Your grandfather used to just pour things together, back before we knew better. I never asked him why he stopped."

"What did he say, when you asked him anything?" Faye said.

Grandma smiled and handed Aubrey a warm towel from the dryer, still soft and heavy, and Aubrey folded it in half, and then in half again.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Spanish, "Más despacio, por favor" means "More slowly, please," a phrase that helps learners follow a fast answer.
story:
Carson stood in Callie's kitchen with his phone dead in his pocket and a soccer ball under his arm. The Saturday pickup game was at a field three streets away, and he had never walked there before, because his mom always drove him and he had never once looked out the window.

"My abuela knows where it is," Callie said, towing him toward the living room. "The field behind the rec center. She walks past it every morning."

Callie's grandmother was folding laundry with meticulous care, matching every sock into a neat pair before moving to the next. Callie asked her something in Spanish, fast and easy, the way water runs out of a tipped bottle. The grandmother answered, also in Spanish, also fast, gesturing toward the window with a towel in her hand.

Carson caught one word, maybe "izquierda," which he was pretty sure meant left, and then everything else blurred together like a page turned before he could read it. "Wait," he said. "I didn't get any of that." Callie just shrugged and said, "That's basically what she said. Left somewhere, then a light, then the field." That wasn't enough. If he got it wrong he would wander around until the game was over, and the coach had already told him twice that showing up late was a bad habit.

He was almost ready to resign himself to missing the first ten minutes when he remembered a phrase from Monday's Spanish class. Ms. Takahashi had made the whole class chant it twice, and he had thought it was a waste of time, but now it floated up like something rising through dark water. He took a breath, walked closer to the grandmother, and said, "Más despacio, por favor."

She smiled, slowed down like a song played at half speed, and pointed at the window while she spoke. This time he heard the pieces separate: the street with the yellow house, then left at the light, and the field behind the rec center, two doors past a hedge that grew like green camouflage over the back fence. Left at the light. Yellow house. Hedge. He said it back to her in English, and she nodded and added something with a thumbs-up.

"That was it?" Callie asked, surprised, following him out the door. "You understood her?"

"More slowly, please," Carson said. "That's all it took."

They walked down the street with the yellow house, turned left at the light, and spotted the hedge behind the fence, and somewhere beyond it Carson could hear the thump of a ball being kicked.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In French, "Excusez-moi" is used to get a stranger's attention politely before asking a question, and "s'il vous plaît" means please.
story:
Camille stood at the end of the language hallway with a folded map of the school in her pocket and her heart going like a drum. In twenty minutes, a group of students from Lyon was arriving, and each one would be sent somewhere different: the gym, the library, the art room. Her job was to give directions in French, out loud, to a real stranger.

She had practiced at her kitchen table the night before, and that was where the trouble started. She knew the direction words. Turn left, go straight, second door on the right. But when she rehearsed stopping someone on the street, she began with "S'il vous plaît" and discovered it felt wrong, like knocking on a door with a whisper. Nobody even slowed down, at least not in her imagination. There had to be a way to get a stranger's attention first, before the asking, before the please.

"Want to try it on me?" Marko offered at lunch. He pushed his tray aside. "I'll be a lost French kid."

Camille squared her shoulders. "S'il vous plaît, où est le gymnase?"

Marko walked right past her, pretending to read a poster about the book fair.

"Hey!" she said. "That's not fair."

"It kind of is," Jackson said from across the table. "If someone just says please at me from behind, I don't even know they're talking to me." He mimed staring at a wall. Camille turned that over. The please word belonged inside the request, not at the front of it. So the missing piece was something before, something that reached out and tapped a stranger on the shoulder with words. She tried to categorize what she knew: words that asked for things, words that pointed the way, words that stopped people. One slot was empty.

She found the answer in Ms. Nowak's classroom after the bell, on a laminated sheet of phrases taped beside the door. She read it twice, then hurried back to the hallway where Marko was waiting by the water fountain.

"Excusez-moi," Camille said clearly, and Marko turned around at once.

"Où est le gymnase, s'il vous plaît?"

He grinned and pointed down the hall. "That time I stopped. That time I would follow you anywhere."

When the students from Lyon arrived, a boy with a green backpack stood in the front lobby, turning a schedule over in his hands. Camille walked up, took a breath, and said, "Excusez-moi." He looked at her right away, eyebrows up, waiting. "La bibliothèque, s'il vous plaît?" She unfolded her map and traced the route with one finger, and he nodded at each turn.

"Bonne chance," he said, and headed off down the corridor, green backpack bouncing, toward the second door on the right.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.
story:
Benjamin sat in the back seat of the family car with his shoes on the paper bag of shoes, the one his mother had packed for the seventh day. Seven days of visiting his grandma's apartment, seven days of neighbors arriving with casseroles, and he still had not figured out the rule behind it. His father drove; his mother stared out the window at the wet streets.

"It's called shiva," Marilou had told him at school, three days after the funeral. "It means seven. Seven days after the burial, and everybody comes to the house to comfort the family." Rhys had stood beside her, shuffling his sneakers, and neither of them had known what else to say. Benjamin had mumbled something about his grandfather, his zayde, and the bell had rung, and that was that. He had replayed the moment every night since, wondering whether he should have said more, or less, or invited them.

He had a theory, and it was this: the visitors were not coming for the food or the stories, though there was plenty of both. They were coming because a family in mourning could not measure its own sadness, could not see it the way you could see weather, so the community stood around it like a fence so the sadness knew its edges. He could not prove that. But he could test it. Today, the last day, he would say nothing at all to anyone, just sit in the corner, and see whether the room still held together.
