The car slowed. "Your grandmother left something for you," his mother said, and passed a small envelope over the seat. Benjamin opened it. Zayde's handwriting, shaky, from before the hospital.

"Benji. When I am gone you will want to be reckless, to drive too fast, to skip the sad parts. Don't. Sit through them. Sadness that nobody shares can go the way of the dinosaurs, total extinction, and you'd never notice it happening. Being sad out loud is how we acquire each other. Come sit with your grandma on the last day and don't fix anything. Just be a warm body in a chair."

Benjamin read it twice. So zayde had run the same experiment, decades earlier, and had reached the same conclusion. That was the twist Benjamin had not expected: his theory had a co-author.

Upstairs, the apartment was warm and loud. Rhys and Marilou were already there, sitting on the couch with paper cups of juice, because Marilou had texted them the address that morning without asking. Benjamin did not say hello. He sat down in the armchair beside his grandma, the one zayde always took, and Marilou scooted over and Rhys put down his cup and nobody spoke. His grandma reached over and took his hand and held it the whole hour, and the room held together just fine.

On the drive home, his father asked, "Did you say anything to your friends today?"

"Not one word," Benjamin said, and looked out at the streetlights coming on, one after another, all the way down the block.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Lifting the lid while rice simmers lets steam escape, which can leave the grains undercooked.
story:
Jade's whole family was coming for dinner at six, and she had promised to cook everything herself: rice, curry, and flatbread, all hot at the same time. Mr. Zhu, their neighbour, had lent her his grandmother's recipe card, written in looping handwriting. "The curry takes twenty minutes," she told Jakub on the phone, "the flatbread only five, so I'll make those last. But the rice is the tricky part."

She set the pot of rice on the stove and turned the flame low, the way the card said. The curry went on the back burner, bubbling with coconut milk and turmeric until the kitchen smelled like Mr. Zhu's backyard in August. Her little brother wandered in looking lethargic, slumped over his homework, and she shooed him out before he could stick a finger in the curry.

By minute four, Jade couldn't stand it. The rice gave off no sound, no smell, nothing. She lifted the lid and stared at the pale grains floating in cloudy water. They looked exactly the same as before. She clapped the lid back on, but two minutes later she peeked again, and then again, just to be sure it wasn't burning. A puff of steam curled past her face every time.

When the twenty minutes were up, she tilted the pot. Water still pooled at the bottom, and when she pressed a grain against her tooth, it crunched. "No, no, no," she muttered, chewing the hard little bead. She had done everything the card said. Same water, same time, same flame. So what had changed?

Then she thought about the steam. Every time she had opened the lid, that cloud had drifted up and vanished. Her mom had installed a new fan above the stove last spring, and Jade had watched it suck cooking steam straight up. Steam, she realized, was part of the cooking. She had let it escape, over and over, and the rice had paid for it. She poured in a splash of hot water, put the lid on tight, and this time she sat on her hands and did not look, not once, even when the pot went silent and suspicious.

Jakub and Margaux arrived just as she rolled out the flatbread, flour dusting her sleeves. "Smells amazing," Margaux said, and Jade laughed because she had almost cried twenty minutes earlier. She stacked the flatbread in a towel to keep it warm, scooped the rice into the big blue bowl, and carried everything to the table.

Mr. Zhu came over with a jar of his own pickles and took the first bite. He chewed, considered, and nodded. "The rice is perfect," he said. "And I can see you have no allergy to hard work." Jade grinned and passed him the curry, and her brother reached across the table for the last piece of flatbread before anyone else could.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Copying =SUM(B2:B10) one column to the right turns it into =SUM(C2:C10), because ordinary cell references are relative and shift with the formula.
story:
Kaylee had eleven minutes of lunch left and twelve columns of science data with no totals, because the robotics club meeting had eaten her whole computer lab period yesterday. The data came from a project Kenneth had started before he moved away: counts of a parasite called a tapeworm found in samples of pond water, recorded week by week. Mr. Khan wanted a total for every week and a bar chart by Friday, and Friday was tomorrow.

She typed =SUM(B2:B10) into the cell under her first column and pressed Enter. The number appeared, and it was right. She checked it by adding the column in her head, which took forever and once made her lose her place entirely. Eleven more columns, and only ten minutes now.

Kenneth's old lab partner Reagan leaned over from the next computer. "You're going to type that eleven more times? You'll be here till midnight."

"There has to be a faster way," Kaylee said. She clicked the corner of the cell with the formula, the little square handle, and dragged it sideways along the bottom of her data. Twelve totals appeared at once. She almost cheered, and then she stopped, because the total under her second column looked wrong. Way too big.

She sat back and thought. She hadn't typed eleven new formulas, so something had made them. Maybe the computer had copied the exact same formula into every cell, which would give the same answer twelve times, but the answers were all different. That didn't fit. So the formula must have changed when it moved. She clicked the cell under her second column and looked at the bar at the top. It didn't say B anymore. It said =SUM(C2:C10). One column to the right, and the letters had walked over too.

"They're relative," Reagan said, peering at the screen. "Mr. Khan says that. Cell references, I mean."

"So when it moves, it shifts with it," Kaylee said. "That's why my totals are all different." But the second column was still wrong, and she deduced the reason quickly: a row of water-temperature readings had snuck into her table, so the formula under that column was adding temperatures to nothing useful. The formula was fine; her data was the problem. She deleted the stray row, and every total corrected itself in one blink.

Then came the chart. She highlighted the totals, clicked the bar chart button, and twelve bars jumped up, weeks marching across the screen, weeks with the biggest parasite counts standing tallest. It looked like a real scientist's work, like something Kenneth would have been smug about in a good way.

"You should ask Mr. Khan if you can present it," Reagan said. "You figured out the copy thing on your own."

Kaylee straightened up, feeling assertive for the first time all week. "I'm going to ask right now, before I lose my nerve." She saved her file, pushed back her chair, and headed for Mr. Khan's door.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
story:
The bakery smelled like butter and sugar, and Brooke stood at the counter trying to remember every French word she had crammed on the airplane. Behind the glass case, a row of croissants gleamed like gold.

"Bonjour," said the woman behind the counter. Then came a stream of French that Brooke only partly caught. Something about her, maybe her age, because the woman smiled down at her.

"Je suis douze ans," Brooke said, proud of herself. Twelve years old, family of four, one dog named Pepper. That was her whole assignment from Ms. Reyes: describe your family and pets in full sentences, in French, to a real French person while on the trip. Brooke had even drawn a little diagram in her notebook to illustrate her family, with stick figures for her parents and her little brother, and a scribbled tail for Pepper.

The woman blinked. She said something short and shook her head, then tapped her own chest and said, "Moi, j'ai cinquante ans."

J'ai. Brooke's ears perked up. She had that word in her notes. Avoir, to have. But the woman wasn't saying she had fifty of anything. She was giving her age, wasn't she?

"Attendez," Brooke said slowly, which was one of the few words she trusted herself to say. Wait. She held up a finger, dug out her notebook, and flipped to the page where she'd written her practice sentences. There it was, in her own handwriting: Je suis douze ans. I am twelve years old. Word for word, straight from English. So why had the bakery woman frowned at it and then used to have instead?

The pieces turned over in her mind the way a puzzle piece does when you know it almost fits. Maybe, she thought, French didn't say I am twelve. Maybe it said I have twelve years, the same way you'd say you have two brothers or a dog.

"J'ai douze ans?" she tried.

The woman's whole face changed. "Oui! Parfait!" She clapped her hands once, delighted, and called something toward the back of the shop. A man in a flour-dusted apron leaned out from the ovens, wiping his hands.

"Elle parle français," the woman announced, as if Brooke had done something heroic rather than said one correct sentence.

Emerson appeared at Brooke's elbow, holding a coin purse and a look of panic. "Did you order yet? Because I've been standing over there trying to remember the word for baguette, and I think my brain is extinct. Totally extinct. Nothing left up there."

"You just need food," Brooke said. "And probably sleep. Ms. Reyes says jet lag messes with some hormone that tells your body when it's daytime." She turned back to the counter, gathered her courage, and pointed at the croissants. She tried a full sentence: her family had four people and one dog, a small brown dog named Pepper. Some of the words wobbled, but the woman nodded along and even repeated the name of the dog with a giggle.

When they finally sat on the bakery's one tiny bench outside, croissants warm in their hands, Emerson tore hers in half. "How did you figure out the age thing? That was so fast."

"I didn't know it," Brooke admitted. "I got it wrong, and she fixed me. J'ai douze ans. It means I am twelve, but word for word it says I have twelve years." She took a bite, flakes drifting onto her notebook. "So what else do you think they say backwards? What if there's a whole list?"

Emerson grinned. "Only one way to find out. Order next."

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: In Stephen Toulmin's model of argument, the claim is the point being argued, and the grounds or data are the evidence given to support it.
story:
Isla spread the index cards across the living room carpet, then flattened them like she was dealing a giant hand of poker. On Monday, the tryouts for the debate team would ask every student to build a case on the spot, and Isla had exactly one weekend to figure out how.

The topic was written on the biggest card: every classroom should keep a recycling bin. Easy, Isla thought. She had opinions stacked like firewood. Recycling helps the planet. Kids want to help. Bins are cheap. She read them aloud to the empty couch, and even the couch sounded unconvinced.

Niko arrived at two, Maryam at two fifteen, both clutching granola bars like tickets. "Okay," Niko said, dropping onto the couch. "Dazzle us." Isla stood at the coffee table as if it were a podium. "Recycling helps the planet, kids want to help, and bins are cheap." She sat down, breathless.

Maryam chewed her granola bar slowly, which was never a good sign. "You said three things that sound true. But what if someone just says, no it doesn't, no they don't, and no they aren't? What do you do then?"

"Then I say them louder," Isla said, and everyone laughed, but the laughing felt like a warning. Niko flipped one of the cards over. "My brother did debate. He kept saying this word, claim. Like, every point needs one." He squinted at the ceiling. "And then evidence for it. I think there was a third thing, but I forget."

"Claim and evidence," Isla repeated, writing it. "So a claim is the point being argued, and the evidence is..." She stopped, because Niko's brother's textbook was still in Niko's backpack, checked out from the library and two weeks overdue. Niko fetched it while Maryam guarded the granola bars.

They found the chapter, and there it was, with a diagram like a sandwich. "In Toulmin's model," Isla read, "the claim is the point being argued, and the grounds, or data, are the evidence given to support it." She read it again, quieter. "Grounds. So in a debate you don't just stack opinions, you build on them, like the claim is the house and the grounds are the actual ground underneath."

Maryam was already sorting the cards into piles. "Okay, new plan. Every card goes in a category: claim, or evidence, or junk." Isla picked up her favorite card, bins are cheap, and held it under the lamp like a detective examining a clue. "Claim. Now I need data. What counts as data?" Niko grinned. "Numbers that aren't just you guessing." They spent an hour dismantling Isla's case piece by piece, and it was strange how good it felt to watch it fall apart, because each time something collapsed they knew exactly what to go find to fix it.

By five o'clock Isla had a case she could defend, a phone full of facts about plastic, and a plan to corner Ms. Sutton on Monday. Then Maryam held up the last unsorted card and raised her eyebrows. It was the tryout sheet, and at the bottom, in small print, it said the tryout topic would be announced on the spot. Isla stared at it, then grabbed a fresh stack of blank cards.

"Then we practice the system," she said, "not the topic. Niko, give me something hard." Niko rubbed his hands together. "Dogs are better than cats. And you're on the cat side." Maryam groaned. Isla squared the blank cards on the coffee table and said, "Claim number one: cats are the more objective choice, because they love you whether or not you feed them. Now somebody find me the data."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: The volt, the unit of voltage, is named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.
story:
Logan sat on the lip of the halfpipe with a multimeter, a battery pack, and three feet of wire, while his friends dropped in above him. Billie rolled to a stop beside him and looked at the tangle in his lap.

"Science homework at a skate park," Billie said. "That's a new level of desperation."

"It's not homework." Logan clipped the meter to the wire. "Ms. Smith said if I can measure voltage and current and calculate the resistance, she'll count it as my makeup lab. I failed the first one." He still remembered standing at the front of the room in September, reading out a resistance of two thousand ohms for a wire that everyone knew was about one ohm. The class had laughed. Ms. Smith had not. It was the sort of humiliation that made a person want to redo the whole unit in public, at a skate park, in October, like a bird that returns to the exact same spot every winter. His dad called that migratory. Logan called it stubborn.

He turned the dial to volts and touched the probes to the battery terminals. The screen showed 9.01. Then he wired the circuit, watched the current reading settle at 1.8 amps, and did the division in the dust with his finger. Five ohms. He squinted at it. That contradicted what he'd written in class, where he'd somehow divided backwards and gotten a number so large the wire would have glowed.

"Volt," said Adelie, who had coasted over and was reading the battery label upside down. "That's the guy's name, you know. Alessandro Volta. The volt is named after him." She pointed at the little word printed under the 9. "We saw it on a museum exhibit about batteries last summer. Big letters, VOLTA, with his picture."

"An Italian physicist has his name on my battery," Logan said.

"And on your failed lab," Billie said.

Logan ignored this. He tested the idea that had been bugging him since September, that the wire itself, not the battery, set the resistance. He swapped in a shorter piece of wire, kept the same battery, and measured again. Same voltage, higher current. The division came out smaller. The wire was the hidden thing, the part you couldn't see, and the numbers found it anyway. He brushed the dust clean and wrote the result on the back of his hand.

Billie dropped into the halfpipe and carved a long arc up the far wall. Logan packed the meter, stood, and rolled to the edge.

"Tell Ms. Smith the Italian physicist and I worked it out," he said, and pushed off.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': preparing and measuring every ingredient before you start cooking.
story:
Brooklyn stared at the three recipes on her station: rice, curry, flatbread, all due on the table at the same time by the end of class. Her first attempt had ended badly. She had set the onions frying, then gone hunting through the spice drawer for cumin while Haroun measured flour beside her, and when she turned back, the onions were black and smoking. The whole curry had tasted like char. "You have to watch onions every second," Haroun said, scraping the ruined pan into the trash. "You can't look away." But Brooklyn wasn't sure looking away was the real problem.

She thought about it while Mr. Santos-Reyes walked between the stations. It wasn't that she was careless. It was that every time she needed something, she had to stop and search for it. The searching was the hidden cause. What if she got everything out first, measured and chopped and lined up, before a single flame was lit? Then nothing would make her turn away. She spread the idea to Lennon at the next station, who was already mixing her dough. "Try it," Lennon said. "Set everything out first. Bowls of spice, chopped onion, everything." Lennon's enthusiasm was contagious, and soon Haroun was measuring his ginger into a tiny dish too.

"Mr. Santos-Reyes," Brooklyn called, "my gran says a word for this. Mise en place. It's French for putting in place, getting every ingredient ready before you cook." He grinned and gave her station a thumbs up, because that was the whole idea, and she didn't need more explanation than that. Her mother used the same word, and Brooklyn had never understood it until now.

Her second attempt had a shaky start. The flatbread dough was too sticky, so she worked in more flour a spoonful at a time, and by the time it rested smooth and elastic, the rice water was already boiling. She counted backward on her fingers. Rice took twenty minutes, the curry simmered fifteen, and each flatbread needed only two minutes in the hot pan, so bread last, curry next, rice first. She lined up her little dishes like soldiers: turmeric, cumin, salt, coconut milk, onion, garlic.

This time, when the onions hit the oil, her hands never stopped moving. Cumin went in from its waiting dish, then garlic, then the curry powder, all without her eyes leaving the pan. The onions turned golden, then soft and sweet. She built the curry on that foundation, pouring in coconut milk and letting it bubble while she patted the first flatbread flat.

At the end of class the three dishes arrived together, steam rising from all of them at once. Haroun tore a piece of bread and dragged it through her curry. "Better than last week," he said, and went back for more. Brooklyn scooped the last grain of rice onto her plate and ate it.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Distracting, such as changing the subject or starting a new game, can interrupt teasing without challenging the teaser directly.
story:
The note was folded into a square and tucked inside Jeremy's lunch bag, which meant Grandpa had written it, because nobody else hid messages in his food. "Bake day Saturday," it read. "Bring your friend Reed if he can come. We need a taster." Grandpa's house smelled like cinnamon all Saturday morning, and Jeremy liked it there because nobody rushed anything.

Reed arrived just after ten, cheeks red from biking. They measured flour and cracked eggs, and Grandpa let them each conceal one surprise ingredient in their own small cake, though Jeremy's was only cinnamon, same as always. It was while the cakes were in the oven that Ariya from their class knocked on the door; she lived two streets over and had seen Reed's bike tipped in the yard.

Ariya came in, but she went quiet fast, because Reed's shoulders had already tightened. Jeremy knew why. At school a boy in their grade called Reed "Dusty" every time he dropped something, and Reed dropped things a lot, and yesterday it had been a whole tray in the cafeteria. Everyone had laughed. Ariya had laughed too, a small reflex laugh, and Reed had seen it.

"Your cakes smell amazing," Ariya said, trying to make it normal again.

"They're for the county fair," Reed said. "Grandpa says if we win, we split the prize."

"Grandpa?" Ariya raised an eyebrow. "Since when is your grandpa fair judges?"

Jeremy watched Reed's face go careful, the way it did when someone was about to tease him about something, even lightly, even kindly. He remembered the cafeteria and how he'd stood there doing nothing, and how telling the boy to knock it off had only made it louder when a girl tried it last month. He needed a different move.

"Timer!" Jeremy shouted, even though the timer had another four minutes. He yanked the oven open, and the wave of hot sugary air filled the kitchen. "Reed, yours is the one with the crack on top, we have to name that cake. It looks like a canyon."

"It looks like your equation homework," Reed said, grinning now, and they spent the whole rest of the bake arguing about canyon names. Ariya wrote "Fort Cake" on the entry form in her neatest printing and said it was a legitimate team entry now, since she'd named it.

Walking home later with the cakes boxed and balanced between them, Ariya said, "Hey, Reed. About the cafeteria. I shouldn't have laughed. That was dumb of me."

Reed kept his eyes on the box. "Okay," he said. "Thanks."

Jeremy shifted his side of the load. "Fair's in two weeks," he said. "Fort Cake doesn't bake itself."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
story:
Aaron stood in his uncle's living room with the practice book open to page fourteen. His bar mitzvah was in three weeks, and he had promised to chant his portion perfectly by Sunday. He ran his finger under the letters and hummed the melody, the one printed in neat little symbols above the words. His cousin Isha sat on the rug doing a puzzle, and she hummed along after the third repetition.

"You're going to sing that in your sleep," Isha said.

"Maybe that's the plan," Aaron said. "If I chant it in my sleep, I can't get it wrong awake." He stopped at one line, though. The symbols stacked above one word looked wrong. He had practiced that phrase with a rising tune, but the printed marks here showed a dip, then a leap. He flipped back and forth between two pages, frowning.

At the rehearsal on Thursday, Mr. Holloway, who led services, unrolled the Torah scroll on the big wooden desk. Aaron leaned in, ready to match his book to the real thing, and then he went completely still. The scroll had letters, rows and rows of them, and nothing else. No vowels. None of the little melody marks. He turned his book sideways as if that would help, then looked up at Mr. Holloway, who only raised an eyebrow and waited.

"Where did they go?" Aaron asked.

"Where did what go?"

"The marks. The tune. It's all blank up here." He pointed at the space above the letters.

Isha, who had come along, snickered. "Maybe they blew away in the monsoon," she said. She had been going on about the storm forecast all week, insisting the sky over the temple would open up any minute.

Then Aaron worked it out. The tune was never on the scroll at all. It lived in his book and, if he kept practicing, in his head. The person chanting had to supply everything. He tested it right there. He set the book face down on the chair, put his finger under the first line of the scroll, and opened his mouth. The melody came out whole, vowels and all, and he got through four lines before he tripped on a word and laughed at himself.

"I dismissed the whole idea of you doing that without the book," Isha admitted afterward. "That was impressive."

"It's proportional," Aaron said. "Nine days of practicing equals four lines of scroll. At that rate I need about, hmm, a lot more days."

Mr. Holloway rolled the scroll closed. "Same time Sunday," he said. "Bring the blank space in your head, not the book."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
story:
Charlie had exactly eleven minutes of the car ride left to figure out whether she was still going to grow, because tryouts started in twelve and Spencer had just ruined her whole morning.

"He had an X-ray," Elliot said through the phone, which Charlie had propped against the dashboard so her hands were free to hold her new sneakers. They were gloriously durable, all thick rubber and reinforced toes, bought two sizes too big on purpose. "For his wrist, after the skateboarding thing. And the doctor showed him the picture. You know how bones grow longer at the growth plates near the ends? Once those close after puberty, you're done. You never get taller again."

"Done how done?" Charlie said.

"Done done. Spencer asked if he'd keep growing and the doctor pointed right at the plates on the X-ray and said that."

In the back seat, Charlie pulled the phone closer and stared at her shoes. Two sizes too big was only a good plan if her feet, and the rest of her, had growing left to do. She had shot up three inches since last spring, her jeans kept flooding like high-water pants, and she had assumed the trend would continue straight through basketball season and into legend. Now she was doing math. If the plates closed after puberty, and she was already in the middle of puberty, her growing could end any minute, like right now, mid-drive. She needed evidence.

"Dad, am I taller than last month?" she asked.

"You were taller than last month about two weeks ago," her dad said, signaling. "You told me the top shelf was mocking you."

That was data point one. She unrolled her backpack's soft measuring tape, the kind from the sewing kit, and pressed her heel against the seat while the car waited at a light. She marked the top of her head with her finger, then measured down. She would do it again next Sunday, and the Sunday after that, and chart the whole thing. If the numbers climbed, her plates were still open for business. If they stopped, at least she'd know before buying shoes again.

"Elliot, ask Spencer if the doctor said how you can tell when they're closing," she said.

"He said you can't tell without an X-ray."

Charlie chewed on that. An invisible thing, inside her bones, deciding her future, and no way to see it. Fine. She'd track the pattern instead. Her cough drop dissolved against her cheek as she wrote CHART on the back of her hand in pen.

The gym rolled into view. On her keychain, the tiny globe from last year's geography unit spun on its little axis, its painted equator a blur of blue and green.

"Wish me luck," she said.

"Grow," Elliot said, and hung up.

She laced the big shoes tight, shoved the phone in her bag, and jogged toward the doors, already planning Sunday.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that had not been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them.
story:
Ariana spread her homework across her grandfather's kitchen table, which was old and porous with coffee stains that had soaked in over fifty years. Ms. Tanaka had promised a quiz on Monday, and Ariana still could not find the number of protons in an element without counting on her fingers. "The atomic number sits right above the symbol," her grandfather said, sliding a cup of cocoa beside her paper. "That number tells you the protons. Zinc is thirty, so thirty protons. No counting."

She tried it. Carbon, six. Gold, seventy-nine. Neon, ten and she had not needed her fingers once. Then her grandfather went to the shelf and pulled down a science book so old its cover was held shut with a rubber band. "My father gave me this," he said, opening it gently. "See how the table in here is different from yours?"

Ariana leaned close. In her notebook, the periodic table was a solid wall of boxed elements, no empty rooms anywhere. In the old book, there were holes. Blank spaces sat between the filled boxes like missing teeth. "Why would they print it with gaps?" she asked. "Was it a mistake?"

Her grandfather only smiled and turned the pages. "Mendeleev made this table," he said, "a long time ago. Ask yourself why a man would leave gaps on purpose." Then he went back to the stove, humming, which was his way of saying the rest was hers to find.

She stared at the empty boxes. If the table were a mistake, the gaps would be scattered randomly. They were not. They sat in neat rows and columns, as if the boxes around them were waiting for something. She tapped her pencil on the blank square below aluminum. "It's like a parking spot," she said slowly. "You leave the space empty because you know something is coming to fill it." Her grandfather set down his spoon and came to look.

"So the gaps were on purpose," Ariana went on, flipping to the back of the old book, where she found a newer table printed on a single sheet. The empty square below aluminum was filled now, with the symbol Ga. "Gallium," she read. "Somebody discovered it later, and it fit right into the gap Mendeleev left for elements nobody had found yet." She checked the atomic number, thirty-one, and wrote it in the margin. Thirty-one protons, sitting there all along, waiting for someone to look.

On Monday, Ms. Tanaka wrote five symbols on the board and Ariana finished first, her pencil barely pausing. After class, Adonis nudged her in the hallway. "How did you get so fast?" he asked. "Easy," Ariana said. "The table isn't just a list. It's a map, and the empty spaces are the treasure."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin, which is one reason to see a doctor early.
story:
Lauren was supposed to be resting at Grandma and Grandpa's house, but resting was boring, so she was watching the monarch larva on the milkweed in the kitchen window instead. It hung upside down under a leaf, curled into a hook. Grandpa said it would form a chrysalis soon, and Lauren kept a notebook open on the counter, drawing it every hour to see whether anything changed.

Then the fever arrived. It came on fast after lunch, one minute she was fine and the next her teeth were chattering, and the thermometer said 39.2. Grandma pressed the back of her hand to Lauren's forehead twice, as if the number might have lied. "We'll watch it tonight," she said. "If it's still high tomorrow, I'll take you to Dr. Patel in the morning, and if you're not better by the weekend, we'll definitely go."

Lauren pulled the blanket to her chin and thought about that. Something was nagging at her, a fact she'd half forgotten from the health unit Shreya had quizzed her on with flashcards. She texted Shreya, who was home from school for lunch: "that flu med thing, the one with the timing. do you remember?"

Shreya texted back within a minute. "Ya. Prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin. It's one reason to see a doctor early. It was literally on the card, Lauren."

Lauren stared at the ceiling. If the medicine worked best within two days, and her symptoms had started today, then waiting until tomorrow morning was fine, but waiting until the weekend was not. The weekend was four days away. She tried to formulate what to say so it wouldn't sound like she was telling Grandma what to do, because Grandma did not enjoy being told things.

"Grandma," she said instead, keeping it simple, "Shreya says the flu medicine a doctor can prescribe works best if you start it within two days of getting sick. So going early matters. Like, today-or-tomorrow early."

Grandpa looked up from his crossword. "Two days?"

"That's what the flashcard said," Lauren said. "It's one reason to see a doctor early instead of waiting it out."

Grandma stood in the kitchen doorway with her arms folded, and Lauren could almost see her weighing it: the phone call, the waiting room, the drive, against four more days of a sick granddaughter on her couch. She'd been all set to wait until the weekend. "Well," she said at last, unfolding her arms, "that changes things, doesn't it." She picked up the phone. "I'm calling now, before the office closes for lunch. Grandpa, find her shoes."

The call took six minutes. They could come at three o'clock. Grandma wrote it on the calendar in her looping hand, then went to find the car keys, and Lauren heard her say quietly to Grandpa, "Imagine if I'd sat on it till Saturday."

Lauren's fever still burned and her legs ached, but she felt less worried than she had an hour ago, the way a wobbly stack of books feels stable once someone squares the bottom row. She shuffled back to the window in her blanket. The larva had straightened out and gone still, transformed into something smooth and pale, right on schedule.

"Look," she said. "It waited exactly as long as it needed to. I didn't."

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: A straw man argument misstates an opponent's position as something weaker or sillier, then attacks that version instead of the real one.
story:
John had the couch cushions arranged like a courtroom, which his mother had already decided not to ask about.

"Claim, evidence, warrant," Carla said from the armchair, reading off the worksheet Ms. Tan had given them. "Every point needs all three, or the whole thing falls apart."

"I know what they are," John said. "I just can't make them come out of my mouth in that order."

The debate was in three days, and the topic was shorter recess. Their side had to argue for it, which John privately thought was like arguing for homework on Saturdays. Kaliyah was on the other team, and she had spent the entire week looking extremely confident, which was either a bluff or bad news.

"Try your first point," Carla said. "Go."

"Recess should be shorter because a revolution in learning happens when students have more class time." John paused. "That's the claim."

"That's a slogan. Where's your evidence?"

He flipped through his notes, which were meticulous for a boy who usually couldn't find his own shoes. "Ms. Tan's article says schools that added ten minutes of class time raised reading scores. Evidence. And the warrant is that better reading matters more than ten extra minutes outside."

Carla considered this. "That's actually not terrible. Say it like that on Thursday."

Thursday came. The living room courtroom was exchanged for the school library, where Kaliyah's team sat across the table looking polished. John articulated his first point, then his second, and then it was the other side's turn.

"The other team wants to take away recess," Kaliyah's partner announced. "They think children should sit in desks from eight to three with no break at all. No games, no sunshine, nothing. Is that what we want?"

John felt his ears go hot. That wasn't what they'd said. They'd said shorter, like ten minutes shorter. He scribbled on his notepad: shorter = no recess??? Underneath he wrote: no. Shorter means shorter.

When the rebuttal round started, he leaned into the microphone before he could lose his nerve. "We never said no recess. We said shorter recess. They changed our position into something sillier, and then they attacked that instead."

"Straw man," Ms. Tan murmured from the scoring table, mostly to her coffee.

"That's called a straw man," John said, pointing at his notes without reading them. "And our real claim still stands. Ten fewer minutes of recess, ten more minutes of reading, and the evidence says reading scores go up."

Kaliyah's partner opened his mouth, then closed it again. Kaliyah herself gave John a small nod across the table, the kind that meant a fair hit had been delivered and she intended to return it.

They lost on the final score by two points. Kaliyah caught up with him at the door. "Nice callout," she said. "Want to be on the same team next time?"

"Only if I get the cushion with the good armrest."

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: Besides side-angle-side, triangles can be proved congruent by side-side-side, angle-side-angle or angle-angle-side, but three equal angles alone only prove the same shape, not the same size.
story:
The community centre math club met on Thursdays, and in two weeks the team would compete at the regional tournament, which meant George had exactly two practices left to understand congruent triangles. He wanted the slot on the team badly, because his brother had held it last year and everyone still talked about it. Ms. Farah had posted a sheet of practice proofs on the wall, and George copied one into his notebook: two triangles, some sides marked equal, one angle marked, and the instruction to prove them congruent.

Leonard leaned over his shoulder. "It's easy. All the angles are the same, so the triangles match." He tapped George's page with his pencil. "Same angles, same triangle. Done."

Nimrit pulled a ruler from her bag and drew a small triangle, then a huge one beside it, and marked the angles on both. "Sixty, sixty, sixty," she said. "Look. Same angles, but one is tiny and one is huge." She held the paper up so the whole table could see. George stared at it. The small one fit inside the big one with room to spare.

"So three equal angles only prove the same shape," George said slowly, "not the same size. That's why the rule needs a side." He went back to his diagram. The marked sides were the two around the marked angle. "Side, angle, side," he muttered. "SAS." He tried the other problems and found that side-side-side worked on one, angle-side-angle on another, and angle-angle-side on a third, but for those he always needed a side somewhere in the mix. Ms. Farah walked past and set a timer on the desk: ten minutes to finish three proofs before the practice ended.

At the last minute, Leonard was still stuck, staring at his page with his pencil chewing up. George could have let him fail and maybe taken his place. Instead he slid Nimrit's drawing across the table, small triangle and huge triangle side by side. Leonard's face changed as he looked at it. "Shape, not size," he said, and started marking sides on his own diagram. When the timer buzzed, both their papers were done. Ms. Farah collected them and glanced over George's shoulder at the two boys, one pencil still passed between them, the big triangle and the little one still lying side by side on the table.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Squash plants grow separate male and female flowers, and only a female flower, which has a tiny fruit at its base, can grow into a squash after being pollinated.
story:
Every morning before the bell, Tyler raced to the school garden with his watering can, because the Harvest Festival was only three weeks away and Ms. Hosseini had promised a table at the fair for anyone who could bring vegetables they had grown themselves. His squash plant was the pride of the whole plot. It had spread across its mound in a tangle of stems wider than a bicycle wheel, and by the second week of September it was covered in big yellow flowers. Tyler counted them one Tuesday: twenty-six.

But when he searched for squash, he found nothing. Not one. Sylvia crouched beside him and turned over leaves while he counted flowers again, as if the plant might have been hiding a squash out of embarrassment. "Twenty-six flowers and zero squash," she said. "That's the worst commerce deal in history. You paid for fertilizer and got nothing back."

Tyler refused to panic, at least out loud. He started looking closely, because a pattern had to be hiding in there somewhere. He pulled one flower off gently and split it open, then another, then another from a different part of the plant. On the stem end of some flowers he found a tiny green bump, swollen like a marble under the petals. On others, the stem end was flat and skinny, nothing but stem. He lined up six flowers on the bench, perpendicular to the edge so Sylvia could see them in a row: three with bumps, three without. "Two kinds," he said slowly. "Maybe only one kind can turn into a squash."

Justina wandered over from the tomato bed with dirt on her chin. "My grandma calls those male and female flowers," she said. "The squash plant makes both." Tyler stared at his row of petals. Only the female flowers had the little fruit at the base, and only a female flower could actually grow into a squash, but it had to be pollinated first. Twenty-six flowers had opened, and not a single one had become anything. "If nothing pollinates them," he said, "I get flowers forever and squash never."

"So give the plant some help," Sylvia said, and nudged a fat striped bee that had landed on her shoe. Tyler wrinkled his nose. He had never planned a career in bee replacement. But the next morning he came with a small soft paintbrush from the art room, and while Justina stood guard asking whether bee school had a mascot, he dabbed pollen from a flat-stemmed flower onto a bumpy one. He did it to every female flower he could find, marked each with a twist tie, and watered deep so the moisture wouldn't evaporate in the afternoon sun.

Ten days before the festival, Sylvia shrieked across the garden loud enough to make Ms. Hosseini drop her clipboard. Under the biggest leaf, three green marbles had swelled into squash the size of Tyler's forearm. Tyler held one up like a trophy, paintbrush still sticking out of his back pocket, and Justina took a picture for the fair table. "Best trade in the history of commerce," Sylvia announced. Tyler just grinned and said, "Bee school graduates, class of one."
